problem: Demand-driven navigation (DDN) assumes each demand instruction needs exactly one object and ignores personal preferences, so it cannot express realistic demands that need several objects. Existing end-to-end DDN and ObjectNav agents also explore inefficiently in multi-object search.
motivation: Real demands (e.g. hosting a party, a comfortable gaming setup) need multiple objects and user-specific preferences, and maintaining full scene meta-information for task planners is impractical. MO-DDN is meant to supply that meta-information from a single natural-language demand. The paper observes that attribute features can be reused as a shared semantic space to score map regions coarsely and to guide local search finely.
key_idea: Train a VQ-VAE-style attribute model that maps demand instructions and object categories into a shared multi-attribute feature space, then use it both to score map blocks for waypoint selection (coarse) and as initialization for an imitation-learned local exploration policy (fine).
insight: Attribute-similarity scores replace repeated LLM queries for waypoint selection: the LLM branch needs one LLM call per episode versus 5.15 for MOPA+LLM and still outperforms it, while the MLP branch matches it. Ablations show attribute-based coarse exploration beats FBE, LLM and CLIP-score waypoint selection (SR_b 23.82 vs 14.56/13.69/12.51). Removing the VQ-VAE losses or codebook initialization drops SR_b to 18.34/17.36, and the basic/preferred weights r_b, r_p trade off SR_b against SR_p, giving user-controllable preference.
method: MO-DDN benchmark: 300 GPT-4-generated, manually checked tasks over 358 HSSD categories. Each instruction has basic and preferred parts with multiple multi-object solutions. Success is the max fraction of a solution's objects in the Find list, reported as SR_b/SR_p and SPL_b/SPL_p.

Attribute model: an instruction model and an object model, each a frozen CLIP text encoder plus an MLP encoder mapping to k1/k2 attribute features. A 128x768 codebook is initialized by K-means on CLIP features of GPT-4 language-grounding attributes. Five losses: attribute MSE, VQ, commitment, reconstruction, and a matching loss on the closest instruction-object attribute pair (weights 2/1/0.25/1/1).

Coarse exploration: builds a point cloud from RGB-D and pose, labels it with GLEE detections, and splits it into 2 m x 2 m blocks. Each block is scored by r_p*max cosine(pref attrs, object attrs) + r_b*max cosine(basic attrs, object attrs), summed over its objects. Instruction attributes come from GPT-4 (LLM branch) or the Ins MLP encoder (MLP branch). A random point in the top-scoring unvisited block becomes the waypoint, reached with the Habitat greedy planner.

Fine exploration: an end-to-end policy initialized from the two MLP encoders, using CLIP visual object features. A 6-layer Transformer with a CLS token fuses instruction and object attributes, then GPS+compass and the previous action feed a 2-layer LSTM actor. Trained by imitation on ~50k short trajectories (avg 9.19 steps) that each end in one Find.

Switching loop: alternate coarse waypoint selection and fine local search until n_find=5 Find actions or 300 steps. Weights r_b and r_p can be adjusted by the user to prioritize basic or preferred solutions.

setting.backbone: CLIP ViT-L/14 text encoder (frozen) + trained MLP attribute encoders + Transformer/LSTM fine policy; GLEE detector; GPT-4 (gpt-4-0125-preview, frozen) for attribute parsing in the LLM branch
setting.training_data: Attribute model: GPT-4-generated language-grounding tasks and attributes. Fine policy: ~50,000 imitation trajectories on 270 seen HSSD tasks in seen scenes. Tasks: 300 GPT-4-generated MO-DDN tasks.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + GPS/compass (pose), plus a natural-language demand instruction
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: MoveAhead 0.25 m, RotateLeft/Right 30°, LookUp/Down 30°, Find, Done (waypoints reached via the Habitat greedy planner)
setting.privileged: none for C2FAgent (Find is resolved by the simulator using GT objects within 1 m in view); baselines MOPA+LLM and FBE+LLM use GT semantic labels to decide Find

numbers_note: The paper defines its own MO-DDN benchmark with four setting combinations (seen/unseen scene x seen/unseen task); the split field is mapped approximately (unseen scene+unseen task -> val-unseen, seen scene -> val-seen). Other combinations (Unseen Scene/Seen Task: SR_b 23.06, SR_p 15.98, SPL_b 6.52, SPL_p 5.11; MLP branch on other settings) are in Table 1. Values are mean over seeds; standard deviations are omitted here.
results: C2FAgent (LLM branch) outperforms nearly all baselines: in Seen Scene/Seen Task it reaches SR_b 23.82 vs 18.61 for MOPA+LLM (which uses GT semantic labels) and 8.10 for DDN. Unseen Scene/Unseen Task SR_b is 15.88 vs 10.33 for MOPA+LLM. The MLP branch, with no LLM, is comparable to MOPA+LLM. Only a few cells are lost, e.g. SR_p in Seen Scene/Unseen Task, where MOPA+LLM leads (10.22 vs 8.65).
limitations: Fixed numbers of attributes (k1, k2) for instructions and objects, which is less flexible than real life.
The agent cannot decide Done early; it keeps exploring until 5 Finds or 300 steps, which hurts SPL.
Evaluation only in simulation (HSSD), with only 30 unseen test tasks and a simulator-assisted Find action; no real-robot tests.
